planting.note: Set small bulbs or bulbil offsets 2 inches deep in humus-rich soil under deciduous trees in early autumn; colonies spread quickly by bulbil, so site where spreading is welcome.

directions: Set small bulbs or bulbil offsets 2 inches deep in humus-rich soil under deciduous trees in early autumn, where they will naturalize alongside bluebells and other spring ephemerals. Because flower heads produce clusters of tiny bulbils instead of true seed, colonies spread quickly and can become assertive groundcover in favorable shaded sites, so site it where spreading is welcome. The mild, garlicky strap-shaped leaves emerge in late winter and are harvested young for salads or as a ramp substitute before the plant goes dormant in summer. Give it consistent moisture through spring growth and let beds go dry once foliage yellows.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Direct sow or set divisions in average, well-drained soil once the ground has warmed in spring; divide congested clumps every three to four years.

directions: Direct sow or set divisions in average, well-drained soil once the ground has warmed in spring, spacing clumps to allow the twisting, chive-like foliage room to fan outward. It tolerates light woodland-edge shade far better than most culinary onions and forms a tidy, long-lived edging clump rather than spreading aggressively. Leaves and the late-summer lilac-pink flower heads are both edible with a mild, chive-like bite, making it useful as both a garnish plant and a low border feature. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to keep vigor up.

planting.note: Sow seed or plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in a site with morning sun and afternoon shade.

directions: Sow seed or plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in a site with morning sun and afternoon shade, since this Siberian steppe native colors up best when protected from the harshest midday heat. Flower buds nod distinctively as they emerge before straightening into dense, rounded pink-purple umbels in mid to late summer, well after most other alliums have finished. Both the blue-green strap leaves and the flowers are edible with a clean onion flavor, and the clumps are useful for filling gaps in partly shaded herb borders. Established plants are quite drought-tolerant but perform best with even moisture during active growth.

subcategory: wild edible shoots / native climbing vine

planting.note: Plant root divisions in spring in rich, moisture-retentive soil at a woodland edge or shaded fence line where the tendril-climbing vine can scramble over shrubs or low structures.

directions: Plant root divisions in spring in rich, moisture-retentive soil at a woodland edge or shaded fence line where the tendril-climbing vine can scramble over shrubs or low structures. Unlike its thorny greenbrier relatives, this species is unarmed and herbaceous, dying back to its tuberous rootstock each winter and resprouting reliably each spring. Young emerging shoots are harvested and cooked like asparagus in early spring before the tendrils toughen, while the small, unshowy flowers give off a carrion-like scent that draws fly pollinators later in the season. It spreads slowly by rhizome and is best left undisturbed once established.

planting.note: Plant dormant hardwood cuttings or bare-root stock in fall along a shaded, consistently moist site such as a streambank planting or the north side of a building.

directions: Plant dormant hardwood cuttings or bare-root stock in fall along a shaded, consistently moist site such as a streambank planting or the north side of a building, mimicking the understory ravines this Pacific Northwest native calls home. The tall, upright canes carry long drooping racemes of small black currants that ripen through summer, with foliage that releases a distinctly musky, skunky aroma when brushed against or crushed. Berries are tart and best cooked into jams or sauces rather than eaten fresh, and the shrub also serves as valuable cover and forage for wildlife. Keep the root zone consistently damp, since it struggles in dry shade despite tolerating low light well.
